title: The maple is a chunky red cube cluster on a thick dark trunk jammed against the
instruction: Move the maple out into the garden at least 3 blocks from the house. Replace the solid red mass with a thinner trunk and an irregular canopy of red and orange leaf blocks, with gaps and a few hanging leaf blocks to break the cube silhouette.
why: The maple now stands free on its own grass patch instead of jamming against the house wall, so its red crown no longer competes with the roofline and the tea house's silhouette reads cleanly. The new lawn grounds the tree in the garden without adding any floating or broken pieces.

title: The roof is a heavy, flat-topped deepslate-tile lid with a stepped, blocky edge.
instruction: Use the hip-and-gable roof preset with stair-and-slab courses and an upturn at the four corners and along the eave line. Replace the ridge spike with a flat ridge cap and add a visible gable (irimoya) end. Mix a few tile shades to break up the dark slab.
why: The roof still reads as a dark, heavy block lid with a stair-stepped edge, so the flat-lid problem is not fixed. The after view adds jagged bumps on the top surface that read as clutter rather than a curved hip or upswept eave, which roughly offsets any gain.

title: The roof overhang is so deep that it hides almost the whole wall. The sliding pa
instruction: Pull the roof overhang in by 1 block, or raise the wall height by 1. Run continuous shoji bays (white panels framed by dark trapdoors or stripped logs) on the front and sides. Add a visible sliding door in the front centre.

title: The footings and veranda are rough. Stone footings are thin, gaps under the floo
instruction: Fill the under-floor gaps with a continuous cobblestone or stone-brick footing course. Lay a clear stepping-stone path of stone slabs from the front edge to the engawa steps. Make the lantern a clear stone-wall post with a lantern on top, placed beside the path.
why: The footings now form a continuous stone base under the floor instead of thin separated blocks with open gaps, and the stone lantern reads as a solid, deliberate column rather than a thin stub, with no floating or clashing bits.

title: Dark roof, dark timber and dark posts merge into one heavy mass. The red maple i
instruction: Use a lighter timber (stripped spruce or oak) for the engawa floor and frame. Keep the dark roof as contrast, and let the maple use red, orange and a little green to blend with the garden greens.
why: The maple moves from a flat dark red blob to a red-and-orange canopy, which reads as an autumn maple and adds warm contrast to the dark roof and timber, though a small green leaf fragment near its top right looks slightly stray.
